title: Oral direct thrombin inhibitors or oral factor Xa inhibitors versus conventional anticoagulants for the treatment of pulmonary embolism.
research_query: What is the comparative efficacy and safety of oral direct thrombin inhibitors (DTIs) or oral factor Xa inhibitors versus conventional anticoagulants for the long-term treatment of pulmonary embolism?
ground_truth_report: The evidence suggests that there is probably little or no difference between direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), including oral direct thrombin inhibitors (DTIs) and oral factor Xa inhibitors, and conventional anticoagulation in preventing recurrent pulmonary embolism (PE), recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE), deep vein thrombosis (DVT), all-cause mortality, and major bleeding. The certainty of the evidence is moderate for most outcomes, with some outcomes rated as low certainty due to imprecision and heterogeneity. The studies reviewed were of good methodological quality overall, but the low number of events and clinical heterogeneity contributed to the downgrading of evidence certainty. Future large-scale clinical trials are needed to determine whether individual drugs differ in their effectiveness and bleeding risk, as well as to explore potential differences in subgroups, such as individuals with cancer or obesity.

title: Treatment of dental and orthodontic complications in thalassaemia.
research_query: What is the effectiveness of photodynamic therapy as an adjuvant to full-mouth ultrasonic scaling compared to full-mouth ultrasonic scaling alone for the treatment of gingivitis in individuals with thalassaemia?
ground_truth_report: This review evaluated the effectiveness of photodynamic therapy as an adjuvant to conventional full-mouth ultrasonic scaling for the treatment of gingivitis in individuals with thalassaemia. The evidence, derived from a single randomized controlled trial, suggests that the combination of full-mouth ultrasonic scaling and photodynamic therapy may lead to improved gingival index scores and reduced bleeding on probing after 12 weeks compared to full-mouth ultrasonic scaling alone. However, the certainty of this evidence is very low due to the unclear risk of bias, the limited sample size, and the short follow-up period. Additionally, the study did not report on the safety or adverse effects of the intervention. As a result, no definitive clinical recommendations can be made based on the current evidence. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of various treatment modalities for dental and orthodontic complications in individuals with thalassaemia.

title: Early vitrectomy for exogenous endophthalmitis following surgery.
research_query: What is the effectiveness of early pars plana vitrectomy combined with intravitreal antibiotics compared to vitreous tap and intravitreal antibiotics alone in the acute management of exogenous endophthalmitis following surgery?
ground_truth_report: The review assessed the role of early pars plana vitrectomy (VIT) combined with intravitreal antibiotics versus vitreous tap biopsy (TAP) with intravitreal antibiotics in managing exogenous endophthalmitis. Based on a single randomized controlled trial, there was very low-certainty evidence suggesting no statistically significant difference in visual acuity outcomes between the VIT and TAP groups at three or nine months. Low-certainty evidence indicated a similar requirement for additional surgical procedures between the two groups. Adverse effects were reported in both groups, including dislocated intraocular lenses and macular infarction in the VIT group, and expulsive hemorrhage in the TAP group. Quality of life and mean change in visual acuity were not reported. The findings highlight the need for further randomized studies, particularly in light of advancements in surgical techniques, to better understand the role of early vitrectomy in this condition.

title: Periodontal therapy for primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease in people with periodontitis.
research_query: What are the effects of periodontal therapy, including scaling and root planning with or without antibiotics, on the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease in individuals with chronic periodontitis?
ground_truth_report: The review investigated the effects of periodontal therapy on the prevention of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in individuals with chronic periodontitis. For primary prevention in individuals with periodontitis and metabolic syndrome, very low-certainty evidence from one study was inconclusive regarding the effects of scaling and root planning combined with antibiotics compared to supragingival scaling. The study reported a potential increase in cardiovascular events, but the evidence was not robust enough to draw definitive conclusions. For secondary prevention in individuals with chronic periodontitis and existing CVD, the available evidence was insufficient to determine the effects of periodontal therapy. The included study did not provide reliable data on key outcomes such as all-cause death or CVD-related death. Overall, the evidence is of very low certainty, and further high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to assess the potential role of periodontal therapy in preventing the occurrence or recurrence of CVD.

title: Nirmatrelvir combined with ritonavir for preventing and treating COVID-19.
research_query: What is the effectiveness and safety of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir in preventing and treating COVID-19 in outpatient and inpatient settings, as well as in pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis scenarios?
ground_truth_report: The review provides low-certainty evidence that nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, when combined with standard care, may reduce all-cause mortality and the risk of hospital admission or death within 28 days in unvaccinated individuals with mild symptomatic COVID-19 who are at high risk of severe disease. The intervention may also reduce serious adverse events compared to standard care with placebo. However, it likely has little to no effect on treatment-emergent adverse events and may increase treatment-related adverse events such as dysgeusia and diarrhea. The evidence suggests that nirmatrelvir/ritonavir probably decreases the likelihood of discontinuation due to adverse events. No evidence was found regarding its effectiveness in improving clinical status, quality of life, or viral clearance. Additionally, no studies were available to assess its use in hospitalized patients with moderate to severe COVID-19 or for the prevention of SARS-CoV-2 infection in pre-exposure or post-exposure prophylaxis scenarios. Equity analyses showed no significant differences in outcomes based on age, but effects favored treatment in White participants, with insufficient data for other subgroups. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and to evaluate the intervention in broader populations and settings.

title: Stem cell transplantation for systemic sclerosis.
research_query: What are the benefits and harms of autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) compared to cyclophosphamide for the treatment of systemic sclerosis, specifically for non-myeloablative selective HSCT, myeloablative selective HSCT, and non-myeloablative non-selective HSCT?
ground_truth_report: Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) shows promise as a treatment for systemic sclerosis (SSc) when compared to cyclophosphamide, with varying levels of evidence depending on the HSCT modality. Non-myeloablative selective HSCT and myeloablative selective HSCT demonstrated moderate-certainty evidence for improved event-free survival and skin thickness reduction. Non-myeloablative selective HSCT also showed improved functional ability, though the certainty of evidence was low. However, both modalities were associated with higher rates of serious adverse events compared to cyclophosphamide, necessitating careful risk-benefit considerations. Evidence for non-myeloablative non-selective HSCT is limited and of low certainty, with some indications of improvement in skin scores and functional outcomes but a high risk of bias. Overall, while selective HSCT modalities appear promising, they carry significant risks, including early treatment-related mortality, and further research is needed to clarify their role in SSc management, particularly in comparison to newer first-line treatments like mycophenolate mofetil and in populations with significant comorbidities.

title: Certolizumab pegol for maintenance of medically induced remission in Crohn's disease.
research_query: What is the efficacy and safety of certolizumab pegol for maintaining medically induced remission in adults with Crohn's disease compared to placebo?
ground_truth_report: Certolizumab pegol (CZP) likely reduces the risk of failure to maintain clinical remission and response at 26 weeks in adults with Crohn's disease who have achieved remission through induction therapy. Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that CZP reduces the risk of failure to maintain clinical remission by 27% compared to placebo, with a number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) of 5. Similarly, CZP reduces the risk of failure to maintain clinical response by 42% compared to placebo, with an NNTB of 4. The evidence for these outcomes was judged to be of moderate certainty due to the low number of events. Regarding safety, low-certainty evidence suggests that CZP may not significantly differ from placebo in the risk of serious adverse events. However, the available evidence is limited to a 26-week follow-up period and does not include pediatric populations. Further research is needed to assess the long-term efficacy and safety of CZP and its applicability to children.

title: Exercise versus airway clearance techniques for people with cystic fibrosis.
research_query: What is the effectiveness of exercise compared to other airway clearance techniques (ACTs) in improving respiratory function and clinical outcomes in individuals with cystic fibrosis?
ground_truth_report:
This review assessed the effectiveness of exercise as an airway clearance technique (ACT) compared to other ACTs in individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). The evidence was derived from four randomized controlled trials, which included participants with varying disease severity and age ranges. The studies compared exercise alone or in combination with other ACTs to alternative ACTs, such as active cycle of breathing technique (ACBT), postural drainage and percussion (PD&P), and underwater positive expiratory pressure (uPEP). 

The findings were inconclusive due to the very low certainty of evidence, which was downgraded because of small sample sizes and high or unclear risks of bias. For exercise compared to ACBT, no significant changes in primary outcomes, such as forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV₁), were observed, and no adverse events were reported. Similarly, for exercise combined with PD&P versus PD&P alone, the results were inconsistent, with one trial reporting a greater increase in FEV₁ with PD&P alone at two weeks, while another trial reported a greater increase with the combination at six months. No adverse events were reported, and adherence to the interventions was high. For exercise compared to uPEP, no significant differences were found in sputum weight, and no adverse events were reported, though participants found exercise more fatiguing but more enjoyable.

Overall, the review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine whether exercise is an effective or acceptable alternative to traditional ACTs for people with CF. Further high-quality, long-term studies are needed to evaluate the clinical benefits and patient-centered outcomes of exercise as an ACT.

title: Tocilizumab for giant cell arteritis.
research_query: What is the effectiveness and safety of tocilizumab, alone or with corticosteroids, compared to therapy without tocilizumab for the treatment of giant cell arteritis?
ground_truth_report: Tocilizumab, administered alone or in combination with corticosteroids, may improve outcomes in patients with giant cell arteritis (GCA). Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that tocilizumab increases the proportion of patients achieving sustained remission and prolongs relapse-free survival compared to placebo. Additionally, tocilizumab reduces the need for escape therapy, particularly when administered weekly. Evidence on quality of life improvements is mixed, with some measures favoring weekly tocilizumab over placebo. The intervention appears to have a favorable safety profile, with fewer serious adverse events reported in the tocilizumab groups compared to placebo. However, infections were the most commonly reported adverse events. The review highlights the need for further research to confirm these findings and to explore optimal treatment duration, patient-reported outcomes, and economic considerations.

title: Probiotics for the prevention of Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis.
research_query: What are the effects of probiotic supplements, alone or in combination with pharmacological interventions, on the prevention of Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC) compared to placebo or other non-probiotic interventions?
ground_truth_report: The evidence regarding the use of probiotics for the prevention of Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC) is limited and of low to very low certainty. The available studies suggest that probiotics may result in little to no difference in the occurrence of HAEC compared to placebo. The evidence is also very uncertain regarding the effects of probiotics on the severity of HAEC at different grades (I, II, and III). Additionally, probiotics may result in little to no difference in the recurrence of HAEC episodes. Serious adverse events were not consistently reported, but one study indicated no serious adverse events related to probiotics. Overall, the current evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the efficacy or safety of probiotics for preventing HAEC. Further well-designed and adequately powered randomized controlled trials are needed to provide more robust evidence.

title: Brivaracetam add-on therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy.
research_query: What is the efficacy and tolerability of brivaracetam as an add-on treatment for individuals with drug-resistant epilepsy, particularly in reducing seizure frequency and achieving seizure freedom?
ground_truth_report: Brivaracetam, when used as an add-on therapy for individuals with drug-resistant epilepsy, may be effective in reducing seizure frequency and achieving seizure freedom. Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that brivaracetam increases the likelihood of achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to placebo. However, the evidence supporting seizure freedom is of low certainty. The treatment is associated with a slightly higher incidence of treatment withdrawal due to adverse events, with low-certainty evidence indicating a greater likelihood of withdrawal compared to placebo. The risk of experiencing one or more adverse events does not appear to differ significantly between brivaracetam and placebo, based on moderate-certainty evidence. It is important to note that the findings are primarily applicable to adult patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy, as only one study included participants with generalized epilepsy, and none included individuals under the age of 16. Additionally, the studies were of short duration, highlighting the need for future research to evaluate the long-term efficacy and tolerability of brivaracetam, as well as its effects on other seizure types and age groups.

title: Antibiotic therapy for chronic infection with Burkholderia cepacia complex in people with cystic fibrosis.
research_query: What are the effects of long-term oral and inhaled antibiotic therapy on lung function, exacerbation rates, adverse events, mortality, and quality of life in people with cystic fibrosis and chronic Burkholderia cepacia complex infection?
ground_truth_report: This review evaluated the effects of long-term antibiotic therapy for chronic Burkholderia cepacia complex (BCC) lung infections in individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). The included randomized controlled trial compared continuous inhaled aztreonam lysine (AZLI) with placebo over a 24-week double-blind period, followed by a 24-week open-label extension. The study found no significant improvement in lung function, as measured by forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), with AZLI treatment. The median time to the next exacerbation was longer in the AZLI group compared to placebo, but the difference was not statistically significant. Similarly, no significant differences were observed between the groups in terms of hospitalizations for respiratory exacerbations, mortality, quality of life, or sputum density. Adverse events were comparable between the treatment and placebo groups. The evidence was assessed as moderate quality, and the overall risk of bias in the study was deemed to be unclear to low. The review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine an effective strategy for antibiotic therapy in managing chronic BCC infections in people with CF.

title: Chemotherapy for second-stage human African trypanosomiasis: drugs in use.
research_query: What is the comparative efficacy and safety of fexinidazole versus nifurtimox combined with eflornithine (NECT) for the treatment of second-stage human African trypanosomiasis (g-HAT)?
ground_truth_report: Fexinidazole, an oral treatment for second-stage human African trypanosomiasis (g-HAT), was compared to nifurtimox combined with eflornithine (NECT) in a single randomized controlled trial. The study found that while fexinidazole offers significant advantages in terms of ease of administration, avoiding hospitalization, and improving adherence, it may be associated with higher mortality and relapse rates compared to NECT. Specifically, mortality at 24 months was higher in the fexinidazole group, though the evidence was of low certainty. Relapse rates were also higher with fexinidazole, with moderate-certainty evidence supporting this finding. The incidence of serious adverse events at 24 months was uncertain, but adverse events were common in both groups, with no significant difference in overall rates. Despite these findings, the convenience of an oral treatment option may provide substantial benefits in resource-limited settings where hospital-based care is challenging. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and to better understand the trade-offs between efficacy, safety, and practicality.

title: Surgical interventions for lamellar macular holes.
research_query: What is the effectiveness of surgical interventions, such as pars plana vitrectomy with epiretinal proliferation peeling and fovea-sparing internal limiting membrane removal, compared to observation in improving visual and anatomical outcomes for individuals with lamellar macular holes?
ground_truth_report: The review assessed the effectiveness of surgical interventions for individuals with lamellar macular holes (LMH) based on a single randomized controlled trial. The trial compared surgery (pars plana vitrectomy with epiretinal proliferation peeling and fovea-sparing internal limiting membrane removal) to observation over a six-month follow-up period. The findings suggest that surgery may lead to better visual outcomes, with an improvement in best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) compared to a slight worsening in the observation group. Anatomical outcomes, such as central retinal thickness and retinal sensitivity, also improved more in the surgical group. However, the certainty of the evidence was rated as low due to methodological limitations, including selection and detection bias, and the small sample size, which limits the reliability of the conclusions. No adverse outcomes or complications were reported, but data on vision-related quality of life and metamorphopsia were not available. Overall, while surgery may offer superior visual and anatomical outcomes compared to observation, the limited evidence underscores the need for larger, high-quality trials to better inform clinical decision-making.

title: Pharmacotherapy for hypertension-induced left ventricular hypertrophy.
research_query: What is the effect of antihypertensive pharmacotherapy compared to placebo or no treatment on morbidity and mortality in adults with hypertension-induced left ventricular hypertrophy?
ground_truth_report: The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effects of antihypertensive pharmacotherapy compared to placebo or no treatment on morbidity and mortality in adults with hypertension-induced left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH). The intervention, which included various antihypertensive drugs, did not demonstrate a clear benefit in reducing mortality, cardiovascular events, or hospitalisation for heart failure. Both intervention and control groups showed similar rates of serious adverse events and total adverse events. However, there is some indication that withdrawal due to adverse events may be more frequent with antihypertensive therapy. The certainty of the evidence is very low, and the findings should be interpreted with caution. Further high-quality clinical trials specifically targeting individuals with hypertension-induced LVH are needed to provide more definitive conclusions.

title: Recombinant growth hormone therapy for X-linked hypophosphatemia in children.
research_query: Does recombinant human growth hormone therapy improve longitudinal growth, mineral metabolism, endocrine function, renal function, and bone mineral density in children with X-linked hypophosphatemia, and what are the associated adverse effects?
ground_truth_report: Recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) therapy may improve height standard deviation scores (SDS) in children with X-linked hypophosphatemia, as suggested by low-certainty evidence from two studies. However, the evidence does not confirm whether these improvements are sustained over time or significantly different from control groups. The therapy may have a transient effect on serum phosphate levels and tubular maximum for phosphate reabsorption, but the certainty of this evidence is very low. Additionally, rhGH therapy may have little or no impact on alkaline phosphatase levels. Adverse effects were transient and observed in a small number of participants, suggesting the treatment may be well-tolerated, though the evidence remains of low certainty. Overall, there is insufficient high-certainty evidence to recommend rhGH therapy for this condition, and further research is needed to clarify its efficacy and safety.

title: Anti-IgE therapy for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in people with cystic fibrosis.
research_query: What is the efficacy and safety of anti-IgE therapy (omalizumab) compared to placebo or other therapies for treating allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in individuals with cystic fibrosis?
ground_truth_report: The evidence for the efficacy and safety of anti-IgE therapy (omalizumab) in individuals with cystic fibrosis and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is currently insufficient. The only included study was terminated prematurely due to recruitment challenges, resulting in incomplete data. Preliminary findings suggest a higher incidence of serious side effects in the omalizumab group compared to the placebo group. There is a critical need for larger, well-designed randomized controlled trials to evaluate the clinical and laboratory outcomes of anti-IgE therapy, including its impact on steroid requirements, exacerbation rates, and lung function. Until such evidence is available, the use of omalizumab in this population should be approached with caution.

title: Enzyme replacement therapy with galsulfase for mucopolysaccharidosis type VI.
research_query: What is the effectiveness and safety of enzyme replacement therapy with galsulfase compared to placebo or other interventions for treating mucopolysaccharidosis type VI?
ground_truth_report: This review evaluated the effectiveness and safety of enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with galsulfase for treating mucopolysaccharidosis type VI (MPS VI). The findings are based on a single small randomized controlled trial with very low to low certainty of evidence. The review found that galsulfase may reduce urinary glycosaminoglycan levels at 24 weeks compared to placebo. However, the evidence is insufficient to determine whether galsulfase improves functional outcomes such as the 12-minute walk test, three-minute stair climb, or respiratory function, as the certainty of the evidence is very low. Cardiac function was not reported in the included study. Adverse events, including infusion-related reactions, were generally well tolerated and managed with standard interventions, with no deaths reported. The review highlights the need for further research to assess the long-term effectiveness and safety of galsulfase for MPS VI, particularly regarding its impact on functional outcomes, organ function, quality of life, and adverse effects.

title: SARS-CoV-2-neutralising monoclonal antibodies for treatment of COVID-19.
research_query: What is the effectiveness and safety of SARS-CoV-2-neutralising monoclonal antibodies for treating patients with COVID-19 compared to an active comparator, placebo, or no intervention?
ground_truth_report: The review assessed the effectiveness and safety of SARS-CoV-2-neutralising monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) for treating COVID-19. Six randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included, evaluating various mAbs such as bamlanivimab, sotrovimab, regdanvimab, and combinations like bamlanivimab/etesevimab and casirivimab/imdevimab. For non-hospitalised individuals, some mAbs, such as bamlanivimab/etesevimab and sotrovimab, may reduce hospital admissions or death by day 30, with low certainty of evidence. However, the effects on mortality, clinical progression, and quality of life remain uncertain due to limited data and imprecision. For hospitalised individuals, casirivimab/imdevimab combined with usual care likely has little to no effect on mortality or invasive mechanical ventilation requirements, with moderate certainty of evidence. Adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) were inconsistently reported across studies, and the certainty of evidence for these outcomes ranged from low to very low. Overall, the current evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness and safety of SARS-CoV-2-neutralising mAbs for treating COVID-19. Further research, including long-term data and studies addressing the impact of emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants, is needed to resolve existing uncertainties.

title: Tocilizumab for giant cell arteritis.
research_query: What is the effectiveness and safety of tocilizumab, alone or with corticosteroids, compared to therapy without tocilizumab for the treatment of giant cell arteritis?
ground_truth_report: Tocilizumab, administered alone or with corticosteroids, may improve outcomes in patients with giant cell arteritis (GCA). Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that tocilizumab increases the proportion of patients achieving sustained remission and prolongs relapse-free survival compared to placebo. Additionally, tocilizumab reduces the need for escape therapy, particularly when administered weekly or biweekly. There is no evidence of a difference in all-cause mortality or vision changes between tocilizumab and placebo groups. Quality of life, as measured by the physical component score of the SF-36, was improved with weekly tocilizumab compared to placebo with a 52-week corticosteroid taper. Adverse events, particularly infections, were the most commonly reported complications, but serious adverse events were less frequent in tocilizumab-treated groups. While these findings are promising, further research is needed to confirm the optimal duration of therapy and to evaluate additional patient-reported and economic outcomes.

title: Interventions for the prevention of persistent post-COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction.
research_query: What is the efficacy of interventions, such as intranasal corticosteroids and olfactory training, in preventing persistent post-COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction?
ground_truth_report: The review evaluated the efficacy of intranasal corticosteroids combined with olfactory training compared to no intervention (with olfactory training) for preventing persistent olfactory dysfunction following COVID-19 infection. The evidence, derived from a single study, is of very low certainty and does not allow definitive conclusions about the benefits or harms of intranasal corticosteroids. Self-assessed recovery of the sense of smell, measured on a visual analogue scale, showed no clear difference between the intervention and control groups after three weeks of treatment. Data on other key outcomes, such as serious adverse effects and changes in the sense of smell, were not reported. Overall, the evidence is insufficient to determine the effectiveness of intranasal corticosteroids in this context. Further high-quality research is needed to provide more robust evidence on interventions for preventing persistent post-COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction.

title: Stem cell therapy for dilated cardiomyopathy.
research_query: What is the effectiveness and safety of stem cell therapy compared to no intervention, placebo, or granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) in adults with non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)?
ground_truth_report: The review assessed the effectiveness and safety of stem cell therapy (SCT) in adults with non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). The evidence suggests uncertainty regarding the impact of SCT on reducing all-cause mortality, improving health-related quality of life (HRQoL), or enhancing functional capacity (e.g., 6-minute walk test) when compared to no intervention, placebo, or granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF). SCT may result in slight improvements in functional class (New York Heart Association), but the evidence is of low certainty. The risk of procedural complications associated with SCT remains unclear due to very low-certainty evidence. Additionally, while some physiological measures of cardiac function indicate potential benefits, it is uncertain whether these translate into meaningful clinical outcomes. The optimal mode of SCT administration and the specific patient population that may benefit most remain undetermined. Given the very low certainty of the evidence, the use of SCT in this population should be restricted to clinical research settings. Ongoing studies may provide further clarity on the efficacy and safety of SCT for non-ischaemic DCM.

title: Opioid treatment for opioid withdrawal in newborn infants.
research_query: What is the effectiveness and safety of using opioids for the treatment of neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) in newborn infants due to withdrawal from maternal opioid use during pregnancy?
ground_truth_report: The review assessed the use of opioids for treating neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) in newborns exposed to maternal opioid use during pregnancy. Compared to supportive care alone, the addition of opioids may increase the duration of hospitalization and treatment but may reduce the time to regain birthweight and the duration of daily supportive care. When compared to phenobarbital, diazepam, or chlorpromazine, opioids may reduce treatment failure, with moderate to low certainty evidence supporting these findings. However, the type of opioid used (e.g., morphine, methadone, or buprenorphine) may have little or no effect on treatment failure rates. Buprenorphine likely reduces the duration of hospitalization and treatment compared to morphine, but there is insufficient evidence to determine its safety or its effect on time to control NAS. Evidence on the effectiveness and safety of clonidine is also insufficient. Overall, the certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, and further research is needed to establish the optimal opioid treatment for NAS and its long-term safety.

title: Ivermectin treatment in humans for reducing malaria transmission.
research_query: What is the effect of community administration of ivermectin, as single or multiple doses, on malaria transmission in populations living in malaria-endemic areas?
ground_truth_report: The review assessed the impact of community administration of ivermectin on malaria transmission in malaria-endemic areas. The included study, a cluster-randomized controlled trial conducted in Burkina Faso, compared two groups: one receiving a single dose of ivermectin and albendazole, and another receiving the same treatment with additional doses of ivermectin every three weeks. The primary outcome was the cumulative incidence of uncomplicated malaria in children aged five years and younger over an 18-week period. The study did not find a statistically significant effect of ivermectin on reducing malaria incidence. The evidence was judged to be of very low certainty due to methodological limitations, including high risk of bias and inadequate adjustment for clustering effects. Consequently, the review concludes that there is insufficient evidence to determine whether community administration of ivermectin has an effect on malaria transmission.

title: Magnetic seizure therapy for treatment-resistant depression.
research_query: What are the effects of magnetic seizure therapy (MST) compared to electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), sham-MST, antidepressants, or other forms of electric or magnetic treatment for adults with treatment-resistant depression (TRD)?
ground_truth_report: The evidence regarding the effects of magnetic seizure therapy (MST) for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) is currently insufficient. The review included comparisons between MST and electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), but no randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified comparing MST with sham-MST, antidepressants, or other forms of electric or magnetic treatment. Analyses of the available data did not reveal clear differences between MST and ECT in terms of depressive symptoms, cognitive function, quality of life, or adverse events. However, the certainty of the evidence was very low due to methodological limitations, including small sample sizes, unbalanced baseline characteristics, skewed data, and the use of non-validated measures for some outcomes. No data were available on outcomes such as suicide or social functioning. The findings highlight the need for large, well-designed, and rigorously reported trials to better understand the potential benefits and risks of MST for individuals with TRD.

title: Oral antibiotics for chronic blepharitis.
research_query: What are the benefits and harms of oral antibiotics compared to placebo for the treatment of chronic blepharitis in adults?
ground_truth_report: The evidence on the use of oral antibiotics for chronic blepharitis is of very low certainty, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions. Two randomized controlled trials evaluated the effects of oral doxycycline compared to placebo. The results suggest that oral doxycycline may slightly improve some clinical signs, such as tear production and tear film stability, as measured by Schirmer's test and tear film break-up time, respectively. However, the clinical significance of these improvements remains uncertain. The evidence for subjective symptom improvement, such as reductions in ocular discomfort or redness, is also very uncertain. Additionally, oral doxycycline may increase the risk of adverse events, with higher doses associated with a greater incidence of serious side effects. Overall, further high-quality research is needed to establish the efficacy and safety of oral antibiotics for managing chronic blepharitis.

title: Vitamin D supplementation for the treatment of COVID-19: a living systematic review.
research_query: Is vitamin D supplementation effective and safe for the treatment of COVID-19 compared to an active comparator, placebo, or standard of care alone?
ground_truth_report: The evidence regarding the effectiveness and safety of vitamin D supplementation for the treatment of COVID-19 is currently very uncertain. The review included studies that investigated vitamin D supplementation in individuals with moderate to severe COVID-19, as well as those with mild or asymptomatic disease. The findings suggest that vitamin D supplementation may reduce the need for invasive mechanical ventilation in patients with moderate to severe disease, but the certainty of this evidence is low. The impact of vitamin D on all-cause mortality at hospital discharge remains unclear due to very low-certainty evidence. Additionally, there is limited and inconsistent data on the safety of vitamin D supplementation, with concerns about adverse event reporting and measurement. The review highlights substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity across studies, including differences in supplementation strategies, formulations, and participant characteristics. Further well-designed, adequately powered randomized controlled trials with robust methodologies are urgently needed to provide more definitive conclusions. Until such evidence is available, the benefits and risks of vitamin D supplementation for COVID-19 treatment remain uncertain.

title: Oral dextrose gel to prevent hypoglycaemia in at-risk neonates.
research_query: What is the effectiveness and safety of oral dextrose gel compared to placebo, no intervention, or other therapies in preventing neonatal hypoglycaemia in at-risk infants?
ground_truth_report: Oral dextrose gel has been shown to reduce the risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia in at-risk infants when compared to placebo, with high-certainty evidence supporting this finding. Additionally, moderate-certainty evidence suggests that oral dextrose gel probably reduces the risk of major neurological disability at two years of age or greater. It also likely reduces the need for treatment for hypoglycaemia during the initial hospital stay, although it appears to have little or no effect on the need for intravenous treatment for hypoglycaemia or the risk of mother-infant separation for treatment. The intervention does not seem to increase the risk of adverse events compared to placebo, based on moderate-certainty evidence. However, there is a lack of data comparing oral dextrose gel to other interventions, such as no treatment or standard care, and no evidence on its impact on exclusive breastfeeding after discharge. Further research is needed, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, preterm infants, and with alternative comparators or formulations of dextrose gel.

title: Selective oestrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) for endometriosis.
research_query: What is the effectiveness and safety of selective oestrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) compared to placebo, no treatment, other medical treatments, or surgery in the management of endometriosis?
ground_truth_report: The evidence on the use of selective oestrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) for the management of endometriosis is highly uncertain, as it is based on a single small randomized controlled trial (RCT) with very low-quality evidence. The study compared raloxifene to placebo in women who had undergone surgical excision of endometriosis lesions. The trial did not directly measure pain relief as a primary outcome but reported a shorter time to the return of pelvic pain in the raloxifene group compared to placebo. Adverse events, including pelvic pain, ovarian cysts, headache, migraine, and depression, were reported, but the evidence was inconclusive regarding whether raloxifene increased or decreased the risk of these events. Quality of life outcomes showed a statistically significant improvement in mental health quality of life in favor of placebo at 12 months, while other quality of life measures showed no significant differences. The study also reported uncertainty regarding the impact of raloxifene on the recurrence rate of endometriosis and provided no conclusive data on fertility or economic outcomes. The trial was terminated early due to higher pain scores in the raloxifene group compared to placebo. Further high-quality research is needed to determine the role of SERMs in the treatment of endometriosis.

title: Corticosteroids for periorbital and orbital cellulitis.
research_query: What is the effectiveness and safety of adjunctive corticosteroids compared to antibiotics alone in the treatment of periorbital and orbital cellulitis, considering outcomes such as length of hospital stay, duration of antibiotic use, visual acuity preservation, pain reduction, and need for surgical intervention?
ground_truth_report: The review assessed the use of adjunctive corticosteroids in combination with antibiotics compared to antibiotics alone for the treatment of orbital cellulitis. The single included study, involving participants aged 10 years and older, reported no significant differences between the two groups in terms of length of hospital stay, duration of antibiotic use, preservation of visual acuity, pain scores, or the need for surgical intervention. Additionally, no major complications of orbital cellulitis were observed in either group, and no corticosteroid-related side effects were reported, though the assessment of side effects was unclear. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to concerns about risk of bias and imprecision. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness and safety of corticosteroids for this condition and emphasized the need for further high-quality randomized controlled trials to guide clinical decision-making, particularly focusing on different dosing regimens and separate evaluations for children and adults.

title: Surgery for idiopathic epiretinal membrane.
research_query: What are the effects of surgical removal of idiopathic epiretinal membrane compared to no intervention, placebo, or sham treatment, particularly in terms of visual acuity, quality of life, and adverse events?
ground_truth_report: This review evaluated the effects of surgical removal of idiopathic epiretinal membrane compared to watchful waiting or deferred surgery. The evidence, derived from a single randomized controlled trial, suggests that immediate surgery may result in a slight improvement in visual acuity at 12 months compared to watchful waiting, but the certainty of this evidence is low due to imprecision and potential bias. The effect of immediate surgery on achieving significant visual acuity gains is very uncertain, and no participants in either group experienced significant visual acuity loss. Quality of life outcomes were not assessed in the included study. No serious adverse events were reported, although one participant in the immediate surgery group developed chronic minimal cystoid macular oedema. Overall, the evidence suggests that for mild symptomatic epiretinal membrane, watchful waiting or deferred surgery may yield outcomes comparable to immediate surgery. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings and to assess long-term outcomes, including patient-reported quality of life.

title: Interleukin-6 blocking agents for treating COVID-19: a living systematic review.
research_query: What is the efficacy and safety of interleukin-6 (IL-6) blocking agents, such as tocilizumab and sarilumab, compared to standard care or placebo in the treatment of COVID-19 across varying levels of disease severity?
ground_truth_report: Tocilizumab, an IL-6 blocking agent, reduces all-cause mortality at 28 days compared to standard care or placebo, with high-certainty evidence. It likely results in slightly fewer serious adverse events, though its effect on clinical improvement at 28 days is minimal, and its impact on other outcomes remains uncertain. Evidence for sarilumab, another IL-6 blocking agent, is less conclusive, with uncertainty surrounding its effects on mortality and adverse events. Data for other IL-6 blocking agents are currently unavailable. Further research, including individual patient data meta-analyses, is needed to identify patient subgroups that may benefit most from these treatments.

title: Blood transfusion for preventing primary and secondary stroke in people with sickle cell disease.
research_query: What are the risks and benefits of chronic blood transfusion regimens compared to alternative treatments, such as hydroxyurea and phlebotomy, for primary and secondary stroke prevention in individuals with sickle cell disease?
ground_truth_report: This review assessed the effects of chronic blood transfusion regimens for primary and secondary stroke prevention in individuals with sickle cell disease, focusing on children and adolescents with the HbSS form of the disease. For children at higher risk of stroke who had not previously undergone long-term transfusions, moderate-quality evidence suggests that regular red cell transfusions likely reduce the risk of clinical stroke and may decrease the incidence of other sickle cell disease-related complications, such as acute chest syndrome. However, the evidence is of low quality regarding their impact on quality of life, transient ischemic attacks, or all-cause mortality. For children and adolescents already on long-term transfusions, the evidence is very uncertain regarding the benefits of continuing transfusions for reducing stroke risk or mortality. When comparing hydroxyurea and phlebotomy to red cell transfusions and chelation therapy, low-quality evidence suggests that switching to hydroxyurea and phlebotomy may have little or no effect on liver iron concentrations in primary prevention. However, in secondary prevention, low-quality evidence indicates that switching to hydroxyurea and phlebotomy may increase the risk of serious sickle cell disease-related adverse events. Overall, the quality of evidence across outcomes ranged from very low to moderate, with significant limitations due to high risk of bias, imprecision, and indirectness. Further high-quality research is needed to guide clinical decision-making, particularly for adults and individuals with non-HbSS sickle cell disease.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists for Parkinson's disease.
research_query: What is the effectiveness and safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists in improving motor impairment, health-related quality of life, and other outcomes for individuals with Parkinson's disease compared to conventional treatment, placebo, or no treatment?
ground_truth_report: Low- to very low-certainty evidence suggests that the GLP-1 receptor agonist exenatide may improve motor impairment in individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD), as measured by the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part III in the off-medication state. The observed improvements in motor impairment may persist for some time after cessation of exenatide, raising the possibility of a disease-modifying effect. However, the evidence is unclear regarding the impact of exenatide on health-related quality of life (HRQoL), non-motor outcomes, activities of daily living (ADLs), and psychological outcomes. Serious adverse events (SAEs) were reported but were unlikely to be related to the intervention. The effect of exenatide on weight loss was inconsistent, with some evidence suggesting minimal or no effect. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and to evaluate the efficacy and safety of other GLP-1 receptor agonists in this population.

title: Standard versus biofilm antimicrobial susceptibility testing to guide antibiotic therapy in cystic fibrosis.
research_query: Does biofilm antimicrobial susceptibility testing improve microbiological and clinical outcomes compared to conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing in the treatment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa pulmonary infections in people with cystic fibrosis?
ground_truth_report: The review evaluated the effectiveness of biofilm antimicrobial susceptibility testing compared to conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing in guiding antibiotic therapy for Pseudomonas aeruginosa pulmonary infections in individuals with cystic fibrosis. Two multicentre, double-blind randomized controlled trials were included, assessing outcomes such as changes in sputum Pseudomonas aeruginosa density, lung function, risk and time to subsequent exacerbations, and quality of life measures. The findings indicated that biofilm susceptibility testing did not demonstrate superiority over conventional susceptibility testing in improving microbiological or clinical outcomes. Both approaches were found to be safe, and the quality of evidence for the selected outcomes was rated as moderate to high using GRADE criteria. The authors concluded that current evidence does not support the routine use of biofilm antimicrobial susceptibility testing for guiding antibiotic therapy in this context. However, they suggested that biofilm testing might have potential utility in the development of new drug formulations for future clinical trials.

title: Digital technology for early identification of exacerbations in people with cystic fibrosis.
research_query: Can digital technologies effectively predict pulmonary exacerbations in people with cystic fibrosis to enable earlier intervention and improve health outcomes without increasing treatment burden?
ground_truth_report: Digital technologies, such as symptom diaries and home spirometry monitoring, likely enable earlier identification of pulmonary exacerbations in people with cystic fibrosis. Evidence suggests that these interventions may reduce the time to detection of exacerbations compared to routine care. However, they probably do not reduce the number of exacerbations requiring intravenous antibiotics or improve lung function over a 12-month period. Quality of life outcomes appear largely unaffected, with no significant differences observed between intervention and control groups across most domains, except for Weight and Body Image, which favored usual care. The studies reviewed were limited by variability in methodologies, inconsistent definitions of pulmonary exacerbations, and differences in management strategies. Adherence to and sustained use of digital technologies, particularly those involving physiological measurements, remain challenges. Additionally, the cost-effectiveness of these interventions requires further evaluation. Overall, while digital technologies show promise for early detection of exacerbations, their impact on long-term clinical outcomes and quality of life is uncertain.

title: Hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide) for sickle cell disease.
research_query: What are the effects of hydroxyurea compared to placebo, standard therapy, or other treatment regimens on acute events, organ dysfunction, mortality, quality of life, and adverse effects in individuals with sickle cell disease, considering different genotypes, age groups, treatment durations, and healthcare settings?
ground_truth_report: Hydroxyurea appears to reduce the frequency and severity of pain episodes and other acute complications in individuals with sickle cell anaemia of HbSS or HbSβºthal genotypes. It likely decreases the occurrence of acute chest syndrome and the need for blood transfusions, while also improving measures of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) and reducing neutrophil counts. However, there is no consistent evidence of its impact on quality of life or adverse events, and no significant differences in mortality rates were observed. For individuals at risk of primary stroke, hydroxyurea may help prevent life-threatening neurological events by maintaining transcranial Doppler velocities. Evidence regarding its long-term benefits, such as preventing chronic complications, and its risks, including effects on fertility and reproduction, remains insufficient. Additionally, there is limited evidence on its efficacy in individuals with the HbSC genotype. Further research is needed to address these gaps and to determine optimal dosing strategies.

title: Antibiotic therapy versus no antibiotic therapy for children aged 2 to 59 months with WHO-defined non-severe pneumonia and wheeze.
research_query: What is the efficacy of antibiotic therapy compared to no antibiotic therapy in children aged 2 to 59 months with WHO-defined non-severe pneumonia and wheeze?
ground_truth_report: The review evaluated the efficacy of antibiotic therapy versus no antibiotic therapy in children aged 2 to 59 months with WHO-defined non-severe pneumonia and wheeze. The evidence suggests that antibiotic therapy may reduce treatment failure by 20% compared to no antibiotic therapy, although the certainty of this evidence is low. Antibiotic therapy likely results in little or no difference in clinical cure, relapse, or treatment-related harms, with moderate to low certainty of evidence. Mortality was reported in two trials, with no deaths occurring in either group. The findings indicate insufficient evidence to definitively support or refute the use of antibiotics for treating non-severe pneumonia in this population. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to address this clinical question.

title: Interventions for frostbite injuries.
research_query: What are the benefits and harms of different medical interventions, such as pharmacological therapy, topical treatments, or rewarming techniques, for managing frostbite injuries?
ground_truth_report: The review evaluated the effectiveness of various medical interventions for severe frostbite injuries based on very low-quality evidence from a single randomized controlled trial. The trial compared three treatment groups: intravenous (IV) buflomedil, IV iloprost, and a combination of IV iloprost with fibrinolysis using recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA). All participants underwent rapid rewarming and received initial doses of aspirin and buflomedil. Results suggest that iloprost and iloprost combined with rtPA may reduce the rate of amputations compared to buflomedil alone. However, the evidence is of very low quality, and buflomedil has since been withdrawn from clinical use. No deaths or withdrawals due to adverse events were reported, though adverse events such as flushing, nausea, palpitations, and vomiting were common but not analyzed by treatment group. The study did not assess outcomes such as pain, quality of life, or functional recovery. Overall, the evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions, and high-quality randomized trials are needed to establish effective treatments for frostbite injuries.

title: Visual cycle modulators versus placebo or observation for the prevention and treatment of geographic atrophy due to age-related macular degeneration.
research_query: What is the efficacy and safety of visual cycle modulators, such as emixustat and fenretinide, compared to placebo or observation for the prevention and treatment of geographic atrophy due to age-related macular degeneration?
ground_truth_report: The review evaluated the efficacy and safety of visual cycle modulators, specifically emixustat and fenretinide, for the treatment of geographic atrophy (GA) due to age-related macular degeneration (AMD). The evidence, primarily of low to moderate certainty, suggests that emixustat may not result in clinically meaningful improvements in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) or significant reductions in the progression of GA compared to placebo. Similarly, fenretinide showed limited evidence of benefit. Both drugs were associated with ocular adverse events, including delayed dark adaptation and chromatopsia, which were dose-dependent and often led to study dropouts. While no systemic adverse events were definitively linked to emixustat, fenretinide was associated with pruritus and rash. There is some low-certainty evidence suggesting that these treatments may reduce the incidence of choroidal neovascularization (CNV), particularly with fenretinide, but further research is needed to confirm this finding. Overall, the current evidence does not strongly support the use of visual cycle modulators for treating established GA due to AMD, and additional focused studies are required to evaluate their potential benefits and risks.

title: Interventions to reduce body temperature to 35 ⁰C to 37 ⁰C in adults and children with traumatic brain injury.
research_query: What are the effects of pharmacological or physical interventions aimed at reducing body temperature to 35 °C to 37.5 °C in adults and children admitted to hospital after traumatic brain injury?
ground_truth_report: The review assessed the effects of interventions aimed at reducing body temperature to 35 °C to 37.5 °C in individuals with traumatic brain injury (TBI). One small randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 41 adult participants evaluated the use of intravenous paracetamol compared to placebo. The study provided very low-certainty evidence regarding the effect of paracetamol on 28-day mortality, with results showing substantial uncertainty. The evidence was downgraded due to imprecision, stemming from the small sample size, and study limitations, including a high risk of selective reporting bias. The primary outcome of poor functional outcome (death or dependency) and secondary outcomes, such as intracranial or extracranial hemorrhage, abnormal intracranial pressure, or infections, were not reported. Another trial on a physical intervention (advanced fever control using a surface cooling device) was excluded due to insufficient data, as it was only available as an abstract. Four ongoing studies were identified, which may provide additional evidence in future updates. Overall, the current evidence is insufficient to draw conclusions about the effectiveness of temperature-reducing interventions in TBI, and further high-quality research is needed to address this gap.

title: Targeted therapy for metastatic renal cell carcinoma.
research_query: What are the effects of targeted therapies, including TKI-based treatments and immune checkpoint inhibitors, on progression-free survival, overall survival, and adverse events in patients with clear cell metastatic renal cell carcinoma who are naïve to systemic therapy?
ground_truth_report: This review evaluated the effects of targeted therapies, including tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) and immune checkpoint inhibitors, for clear cell metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC) in patients who had not received prior systemic treatment. The evidence suggests that combinations of immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as avelumab plus axitinib or pembrolizumab plus axitinib, are likely superior to single-agent targeted therapies like sunitinib in improving progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). For example, sunitinib was associated with reduced PFS and OS compared to these combinations, with moderate to high certainty of evidence for some outcomes. Additionally, sunitinib was associated with a higher risk of serious adverse events (SAEs) compared to nivolumab plus ipilimumab, although the certainty of evidence for this finding was moderate. Among single-agent targeted therapies, pazopanib and sunitinib showed similar outcomes for PFS, OS, and SAEs, with low-certainty evidence. Overall, the review highlights that combination therapies involving immune checkpoint inhibitors may offer better oncological outcomes and a more favorable safety profile compared to single-agent targeted therapies, though the certainty of evidence varies across comparisons.

title: Behavioural activation therapy for depression in adults with non-communicable diseases.
research_query: What are the effects of behavioural activation therapy compared to various control groups (e.g., no treatment, waiting list, other psychological therapy, pharmacological treatment, or treatment as usual) for the treatment of depression in adults with non-communicable diseases such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer, and chronic respiratory conditions?
ground_truth_report: Behavioural activation therapy was compared to treatment as usual and problem-solving therapy in two studies involving adults with depression and non-communicable diseases (NCDs). The intervention consisted of eight weeks of face-to-face behavioural therapy. Evidence suggested that behavioural activation may improve treatment efficacy (remission) in the short and medium term, with risk ratios (RR) of 1.53 (95% CI 0.98 to 2.38; low-certainty evidence) and 1.76 (95% CI 1.01 to 3.08; moderate-certainty evidence), respectively. However, these estimates lacked precision, and the effects diminished in the long term (RR 1.42, 95% CI 0.91 to 2.23; moderate-certainty evidence). There was no evidence of a difference in treatment acceptability or depression symptoms between behavioural activation and comparators in the short or medium term (low-certainty evidence). Additionally, no differences were observed in quality of life, functioning, or anxiety symptoms, and adverse effects were not reported. The overall evidence was limited by risks of bias and low certainty, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about the efficacy and acceptability of behavioural activation for this population. Further research, particularly in low-resource settings and among individuals with subthreshold or undiagnosed depression, is needed to better understand the potential benefits of this intervention.

title: Inhaled mannitol for cystic fibrosis.
research_query: What is the efficacy and safety of inhaled dry powder mannitol compared to placebo, active inhaled comparators (e.g., hypertonic saline or dornase alfa), or no treatment in improving lung function, quality of life, and managing adverse events in individuals with cystic fibrosis?
ground_truth_report: Moderate-quality evidence suggests that inhaled dry powder mannitol, when used for up to six months, improves some measures of lung function in individuals with cystic fibrosis compared to control treatments. However, the evidence for its impact on health-related quality of life is low to very low quality, with no consistent differences observed except for a temporary reduction in the burden of treatment up to four months. The evidence comparing mannitol to dornase alfa alone or in combination with mannitol is of very low quality, showing no significant differences in lung function or quality of life. Common adverse events associated with mannitol include cough, haemoptysis, bronchospasm, pharyngolaryngeal pain, and post-tussive vomiting, though no significant differences in adverse event rates were observed between mannitol and control groups. The clinical implications suggest that mannitol may be considered as a treatment option for cystic fibrosis, but further high-quality research is needed to identify the subgroups most likely to benefit and to compare its efficacy against established mucolytic therapies.

title: Normal saline (0.9% sodium chloride) versus heparin intermittent flushing for the prevention of occlusion in long-term central venous catheters in infants and children.
research_query: What are the clinical effects of intermittent flushing with normal saline compared to heparin for preventing occlusion in long-term central venous catheters in infants and children?
ground_truth_report: This review evaluated the effects of intermittent flushing with normal saline versus heparin for preventing occlusion in long-term central venous catheters (CVCs) in infants and children. The evidence, derived from four randomized controlled trials, was of low to very low certainty due to high heterogeneity, lack of blinding, and wide confidence intervals. The findings suggest no clear difference between normal saline and heparin in preventing CVC occlusion or CVC-associated bloodstream infections. The relative risk for CVC occlusion per 1000 catheter days was estimated at 0.75 (95% CI 0.10 to 5.51), while the relative risk for CVC-associated bloodstream infections was 1.48 (95% CI 0.24 to 9.37). The duration of catheter placement appeared similar between the two groups in one study, but this outcome was not consistently reported across all trials. Overall, the review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine whether heparin is necessary for preventing occlusion, bloodstream infections, or influencing catheter duration. Further high-quality research is needed to establish clear guidelines for the maintenance of long-term CVCs in this population.

title: Transarterial (chemo)embolisation versus no intervention or placebo for liver metastases.
research_query: What are the benefits and harms of transarterial embolisation (TAE) or transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE) compared with no intervention or placebo in people with liver metastases?
ground_truth_report: The evidence regarding the effects of transarterial embolisation (TAE) or transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE) compared with no intervention or placebo in people with liver metastases is highly uncertain due to the inclusion of only one small randomised trial at high risk of bias. The trial reported inconclusive results for mortality at 44 months, with no statistically significant differences observed between the intervention and control groups. Median survival times were similar across groups, with no clear advantage for TAE or TACE. Short-term adverse events, such as post-embolisation syndrome, nausea, and localized complications, were reported in the intervention groups but not in the control group. The trial did not assess critical outcomes such as failure to clear liver metastases, time to progression, tumour response, or health-related quality of life. Overall, the current evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the clinical effectiveness or safety of TAE or TACE for liver metastases. Further large, well-conducted trials are needed to provide more robust evidence on this topic.

title: Cognitive training interventions for dementia and mild cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease.
research_query: Does cognitive training improve cognitive function, activities of daily living, or quality of life in individuals with Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) or mild cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease (PD-MCI)?
ground_truth_report: This review evaluated the effects of cognitive training interventions on individuals with Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) or mild cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease (PD-MCI). The interventions targeted either single or multiple cognitive domains and were compared to control conditions such as no intervention, recreational activities, or motor therapy. The evidence did not demonstrate clear improvements in global cognition, executive function, or visual processing. While cognitive training showed some potential benefits in attention and verbal memory, these findings were based on low-certainty evidence and were less robust in sensitivity analyses. No significant differences were observed in activities of daily living or quality of life between the cognitive training and control groups. The overall certainty of the evidence was low due to methodological limitations, small sample sizes, and imprecise results. Further well-designed and adequately powered studies are needed to determine the efficacy of cognitive training in this population, particularly for individuals with PDD.

title: Different unfractionated heparin doses for preventing arterial thrombosis in children undergoing cardiac catheterization.
research_query: What are the effects of low-dose (< 100 units/kg) versus high-dose (≥ 100 units/kg) unfractionated heparin administered as an intravenous bolus during cardiac catheterization on the prevention of arterial thrombosis, bleeding complications, and other adverse events in children aged 0 to 18 years?
ground_truth_report: The review evaluated the effects of low-dose versus high-dose unfractionated heparin administered as an intravenous bolus during cardiac catheterization in children for the prevention of arterial thrombosis. The evidence, derived from two studies, was of moderate certainty due to concerns about risk of bias and imprecision. The findings did not demonstrate a clear difference in the risk of arterial thrombotic events between the two dosing regimens, with the confidence interval suggesting potential benefits for either approach. For bleeding complications, one study reported no significant differences in the incidence of major or minor bleeding events between the low-dose and high-dose groups. Similarly, the incidence of deep vein thrombosis did not differ significantly between the two regimens. However, the limited number of studies, small sample sizes, and incomplete reporting of outcomes restrict the ability to draw definitive conclusions. Further well-designed, adequately powered randomized controlled trials are necessary to establish the optimal dosing strategy for unfractionated heparin in this clinical context.

title: Sound reduction management in the neonatal intensive care unit for preterm or very low birth weight infants.
research_query: What are the effects of sound reduction interventions, such as silicone earplugs, on growth, neurodevelopmental outcomes, short-term medical outcomes, sleep patterns, staff performance, and parental satisfaction in preterm or very low birth weight infants in neonatal intensive care units?
ground_truth_report: The review assessed the effects of sound reduction interventions, specifically the use of silicone earplugs, on preterm or very low birth weight infants in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). The evidence is based on a single high-quality randomized controlled trial with a small sample size. The study found no significant differences in weight at 34 weeks postmenstrual age or at 18 to 22 months corrected age between infants who used silicone earplugs and those who did not. However, a significant improvement in the Mental Developmental Index (Bayley II) was observed in the silicone earplugs group at 18 to 22 months corrected age, while no significant difference was found for the Psychomotor Development Index. The authors concluded that the current evidence is insufficient to make clinical recommendations due to the limited sample size and emphasized the need for larger, well-designed trials to evaluate the effectiveness of sound reduction interventions in this population.

title: Interventions for chronic pruritus of unknown origin.
research_query: What are the effects of interventions, including non-pharmacological, topical, and systemic pharmacological treatments, on chronic pruritus of unknown origin (CPUO) in adults and children?
ground_truth_report: This review evaluated the effects of interventions for chronic pruritus of unknown origin (CPUO) in adults and children. The only intervention assessed was the neurokinin 1 receptor (NK1R) antagonist serlopitant, based on a single study. Low-certainty evidence suggests that serlopitant 5 mg may reduce pruritus intensity compared to placebo, as measured by the visual analogue scale (VAS). However, the effects of serlopitant on other outcomes, such as adverse events, health-related quality of life, and sleep disturbances, remain uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. The study did not report on depression or patient satisfaction. The evidence was downgraded due to indirectness, as only 55% of participants had CPUO, and due to imprecision and risk of bias in some outcomes. Overall, there is a lack of robust evidence to guide clinical decision-making for most interventions for CPUO. Further research with larger sample sizes and a focus on patients with CPUO is needed to provide more definitive conclusions.

title: Blood transfusions for treating acute chest syndrome in people with sickle cell disease.
research_query: What is the effectiveness of blood transfusions, including simple and exchange transfusions, compared to standard care in treating acute chest syndrome in individuals with sickle cell disease?
ground_truth_report: The review evaluated the effectiveness of blood transfusions, including simple and exchange transfusions, for treating acute chest syndrome in individuals with sickle cell disease. The evidence was derived from a single, small randomized controlled trial, which included ten participants. The trial compared the outcomes of individuals receiving a single transfusion of packed red blood cells to those receiving standard care. None of the participants in the transfusion group developed acute chest syndrome, while 33% of participants in the standard care group did. However, no data were available for other predefined outcomes. The authors concluded that the evidence is insufficient to draw reliable conclusions about the effectiveness of blood transfusions for this condition. While there is some indication that chronic blood transfusion may reduce the incidence of acute chest syndrome, the current evidence is too limited to confirm the benefits or assess potential harms. Clinicians are advised to base treatment decisions on clinical experience, individual patient circumstances, and patient preferences. Further high-quality research is needed to establish the efficacy and safety of blood transfusions for managing acute chest syndrome in people with sickle cell disease.
